title: Danielsson confirmed as Wild Card for F1 ACADEMY Austin round
excerpt:
F1 ACADEMY has announced that Alexia Danielsson will represent TeamViewer, the series’ Official Partner, as the Wild Card entry for Round 5 of the 2026 season in Austin.

The Swedish racer started racing single-seaters in 2022, moving up from Aquilia Formula 1000 to Nordic 4 two years later and scoring her first victory in the series last season. Additionally, she won on debut in the Porsche Sprint Challenge Scandinavia in 2025, before delivering a points-scoring rookie season in the F4 CEZ Championship this year.

Danielsson was one of the standout performers in last week’s F1 ACADEMY Rookie Test in Navarra, claiming the second-fastest time overall.

The 17-year-old will make her debut behind the wheel of the #45 TeamViewer operated by Hitech car, which will feature a special edition livery showcasing the role of communities in supporting women’s career progression – on and off the track.

Celebrating TeamViewer’s Forward Together campaign, which highlights how being part of formal and informal communities helps women enter and advance in sports and tech roles, the design includes 250 inspiring women.

Those featured represent communities focused on leadership development, advancing women in technology, empowering the next generation in STEM, strengthening professional networks, and driving greater inclusion in motorsport and automotive industries.

"It has been an absolutely incredible few days," said Danielsson. "First, to be given this opportunity by McLaren and then to perform so well at the F1 ACADEMY test was more than I had dared hope for.

"And now it is also official that I will race as a Wild Card in F1 ACADEMY during the United States Grand Prix, which feels absolutely amazing. Racing at COTA in front of such a huge crowd, right in the middle of a Formula 1 weekend, will be an experience I will never forget and something I can build on going forward."

Danielsson spoke further of her excitement at driving during F1's visit to Austin, adding: "More than anything, I’m just really excited to get the chance to race during a Formula 1 weekend. I’ve only been to an F1 race once before, and that was at Zandvoort in the Netherlands a month ago, when McLaren announced me as one of their drivers for the Rookie Test.

"My main goal for the weekend is to learn as much as I possibly can. I’m also competing for a place on the grid for the full season next year, so if I get that opportunity, I want to be as prepared as I can be."

Karin Fink, Head of Commercial Operations, F1 ACADEMY said: “Motorsports has always had a strong community behind it, and this is no different at F1 ACADEMY. The drivers are supported by so many around them, so it is nice to see some of those communities that inspire change for women, both on and off the track, featured on TeamViewer’s livery. By creating spaces where women not only belong but also have the opportunity to engage and share knowledge, we are able to empower more women to advance, no matter the industry.”

Faith Wheller, VP of Brand and Sports Partnerships, TeamViewer added: “Building on our campaign last year where we brought visibility to role models, this year we wanted to do something just as important to helping women advance. Forward Together highlights the need for communities and the role they play in our careers.

“The opportunity to support a young talent like Alexia in her F1 ACADEMY debut while also featuring many women who have supported the next generation in other industries is why this livery is so important. We look forward to being in Austin this October to support Alexia in person.”

title: How Verstappen won the ‘biggest race’ of his motorsport career
excerpt:
Just a few days after recording a podium finish in the Spanish Grand Prix, Max Verstappen was at another track and on the hunt for another trophy – the four-time F1 World Champion taking part in Red Bull’s special ‘Max vs 100’ karting event.

Held at Silverstone on Wednesday evening, the challenge was clear: overtake and eliminate 100 competitors – including Red Bull athletes, content creators and more – from the very back of the grid in 30 laps (or 75 minutes).

Red Bull, who have a long track record of stunts across various sports, described it as “the world’s biggest go-kart race”, with the action being broadcast live on Disney+, covered extensively across social media and treated like a headline encounter.

After a couple of practice days for an enthusiastic field of challengers, overseen by Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad, things became serious when Verstappen arrived to get his first taste of a 2.5km track that blended Silverstone’s kart venue and sections of its F1 layout.

Verstappen’s pace – displayed to devastating effect in F1 over the last decade – was obviously never in question, but would the Dutchman have the time, space and dash of fortune required to pull off an ambitious charge from 101st to first?

“It’s a long way! A very long way!” Verstappen smiled during a pre-race interview as he walked from the front to the back of the grid – the size of the challenge appearing to dawn on him moments before the 1800 start.

What followed was box office entertainment.

Verstappen’s P101 to P1 charge

Shuffling forward in his kart to gain momentum as soon as the lights went out, Verstappen had ducked and dived past a gaggle of rivals by Turn 1, where he somehow managed to avoid being taken out in the bottleneck, and then strategically took to the grass to avoid various spinners.

His rapid rise continued through the rest of Sector 1 and Sector 2, until Race Control threw a Full Course Yellow to cover off further incidents.

It felt like Verstappen had managed to pick off 20 or 30 karts amid the drama. At a push, 40 or 50. Yet incredibly, when the timing screens updated, he found himself in 37th position, having made up a whopping 64 places in just one tour.

“Not a bad first lap, then!” Verstappen chimed on the radio when informed about his progress.

After the racing resumed, Verstappen climbed to 25th by Lap 4, 10th by Lap 6, and fifth by Lap 7, the number of karts out on track dropping and dropping until just three others remained: those of F1 journalist Jacky Martens, YouTuber Zac Alsop and Red Bull Ford Powertrains technician Lewis Osler.

The front three, led by polesitter Martens, joked over the radio about how they might work together to form a roadblock when Verstappen arrived, but in reality, there was no stopping the F1 superstar.

After just 35 minutes, and 14 laps, Verstappen had caught and passed them all.

“That was simply lovely,” Verstappen chuckled over the radio once he had eliminated the final kart, adding that “it’s my first win of the year, so I’ll take this one!”

Speaking to select media, including F1.com, afterwards, Verstappen reflected: “I grew up racing a lot in karts, then because of your formula career you don’t really get a lot of time racing them anymore, so it’s always nice to go back and have a go at it.

“I got three or four laps on the track, and that was basically my practice. Before that, it’s always very hard to know what to expect, so it’s also better then not to overthink the situation, and just feel it once you sit in the kart. But I think the most that I’ve been on a track with is like 40 karts, maybe, so a hundred is a lot!”

Verstappen’s fastest lap of the race was 2m 20.673s, with the next best being a 2m 23.327s from Martens, some 2.6s slower.

“I knew my lap times when I did the prep laps, and I knew the Qualifying lap times of the others, so I knew that it was possible [to win], but it also really depended on my first two laps,” said Verstappen. “They went better than expected, so that of course helped a lot.

“Before the race, I said, ‘Let’s be bold and say that I will pass 40 people in Lap 1’, and then they told me [what it was] at the end. It was a good effort. Some people got really excited on the new [extended] part of the track, and there was a bit of a road blockage going on, but I managed to swerve around it, and it worked out well.

“When the lights go out, you kind of just see where the gaps are, and then you also kind of need to trust a few people around you, that they don’t do anything crazy. To be honest, they didn’t. They were very excited with each other, but they were actually quite nice to me! They weren’t crashing into me or whatever.”

“He sees something we don’t see”

Track Designer and Race Director David Terrien was one of many onlookers at Silverstone who could only smile at what unfolded, with Verstappen’s aggressive approach, differing lines and later braking points visible from the outset.

“Going through the traffic of such a big field, no one has done it,” Terrien commented. “There’s never been a karting race with so many karts. So, even Max was questioning himself just before the start, how he could go through the traffic.

“When you look at the replay, he picked the right spots. Every time there was a gap, he went for it. He was on the right side of the track when there was a crash going on the other side. I think that’s what makes the difference with Max – his starts, and his reaction time. He showed his skills in all aspects.

“I was talking to Max’s race engineer and we were looking at the replay of the start. He sees something we don’t see. He sees a gap that’s going to open, and it’s not open yet. So, I think that’s a race vision. That’s something he has that most of the drivers don’t have.”

For Verstappen, as well as that element of competition, having joked about there being “no mercy” whenever his helmet goes on, Wednesday’s event was another Red Bull exercise that he will keep in mind for a long time – having previously driven an F1 car down a mountain and raced caravans with Daniel Ricciardo.

“Sometimes I get reminded of what I actually did in the past, and I’m like, ‘Oh my God, did I really do that?’” Verstappen said. “It’s definitely one of the best ones out there. I mean, how many times do you have the opportunity to create something like this? Racing against a hundred other people from other disciplines or sports.

“I think it’s great that with Red Bull, they always come up with some crazy, fun things, and it suits me as well. I think also the way that it was organised today… I know it requires a lot of effort to be able to do something like this, and it’s a lot of fun to be a part of that.”

So, could this become a tradition?

“That’s what I said! I was like, ‘Maybe 200’, and then we’ll see again,” Verstappen responded, before signing off from the press conference and enjoying what will go down as one of his most memorable victories.

title: What's new with the F1 Sprint in 2027?
excerpt:
The 2027 Formula 1 calendar is out and, among other things, you will have noticed there are more Sprints than ever before. Here's what you need to know...

How many more Sprints are we talking and why are we increasing?

The Sprint has been a hit and so due to the increasing popularity of the format, there'll be four more than in 2026, bringing the overall total to 10.

Since the Sprint concept was introduced in 2021, data shows that total viewership of Sprint weekends is 12% higher than non-Sprint weekends.

Sprint Qualifying is up to three times more popular with fans than practice (Sprint Qualifying replaces second practice on a Friday afternoon on non-Sprint weekends).

Meanwhile, 82% of attendees at Sprint weekends say it adds value to their ticket with competitive sessions taking place on three days, rather than two on a traditional weekend.

Data also shows 75% of F1 fans believe Sprint events add greater value to a season’s calendar.

As a result, the number of Sprints has risen from three each year in 2021 and 2022 to six each year between 2023 and 2026 with 10 planned for next season.

Gotcha. Will any venues get a Sprint for the first time?

Yes – Bahrain, which hosts the season opener, Australia, Japan, Monaco plus the season finale in Abu Dhabi will all get their first taste of the Sprint format.

Sorry, did you say Monaco is getting a Sprint?

Yep, you read that right. One of the most exhilarating sessions to watch in Formula 1 is Qualifying in Monaco as drivers navigate the tight and twisty streets of Monte Carlo.

Now, fans will get to enjoy not one but two of those spectacular sessions in the Principality.

Sprint Qualifying will take place on Friday ahead of the Sprint on Saturday morning (which replaces FP3) and then Qualifying for the main Grand Prix takes place later on Saturday.

Formula 1 reveals calendar for 2027 season with 10 Sprint events

Okay, so you've mentioned five of the Sprints – what about the other five?

Canada will host a Sprint for the second successive year, with Mercedes duo George Russell and Kimi Antonelli having delivered a sensational battle for the lead there earlier this year.

Silverstone gets its third Sprint after hosting one in 2021 and earlier this year, while Monza gets its second Sprint, six years after the Temple of Speed hosted its first.

Brazil extends its record of having hosted the most Sprints as it returns for the sixth edition at the iconic Interlagos track in Sao Paulo.

Qatar is back with a Sprint too, with Lusail getting a fourth one in five years.

With Abu Dhabi also hosting one, the season will end with back-to-back Sprints, leaving more points available for the final two Grands Prix weekends of the year.

At the other end of the calendar, with Bahrain, Australia and Japan hosting their first Sprints, it sees the season start with three Sprints in the first four race weekends – and that will reward teams who are fast and competitive straight out of the box.

Great stuff. Just remind me about the format of a Sprint?

Of course! As the name suggests, it's a short race. It runs over 100km, which is around one-third of a typical Grand Prix distance. It lasts roughly 30 minutes.

There are no mandatory pit stops like the Grand Prix and, while they are not banned, given the Sprint is so short it's not worth boxing for fresh rubber.

Points are awarded for the top eight positions with eight for the winner down to one for P8.

The introduction of the Sprint means the number of practice sessions are reduced from three one-hour sessions to just one 60-minute run.

Sprint Qualifying is a shortened version of the main Qualifying session, with SQ1 running for 12 minutes, SQ2 for 10 minutes and SQ3 for just eight minutes.

All in all, it means more competitive sessions across a season.

title: Everything you need to know about the 2027 F1 calendar
excerpt:
The 2027 Formula 1 calendar is out – and you'll find familiar faces, returning venues and more Sprints than ever before. Here's everything you need to know...

Okay, you've got my attention. What lies in store next year?

We've got 24 Grands Prix on the cards with Bahrain hosting the season-opener as part of a double header with Saudi Arabia in March.

The teams and drivers will then embark on a global odyssey across five continents, visiting historic venues and major global destinations before arriving at the finale in Abu Dhabi in December.

The calendar runs across 10 months and was created with sustainability in mind, with races grouped together to allow for an efficient geographical flow of events across the year.

And for 2027, as the Sprint format has proved so popular, the championship will raise the number of race weekends that feature a Sprint from six to 10. More on that later.

I can't wait. What's the plan after the initial Middle Eastern double header?

Australia, which hosted this year's opener, moves to race three and is the start of a triple header with Japan (don't worry, it'll still be cherry blossom season when we hit Suzuka) and China.

Then there's a move to North America for the first of three visits to the United States with the Miami Grand Prix.

There's a two-weekend gap before the Canadian Grand Prix with freight going direct to Montreal.

Formula 1 reveals calendar for 2027 season

Nice! When do we get to Europe, then?

That's the next stop! Monaco remains in its new June date and opens the European leg of the season, with Portugal returning to the calendar after signing a two-year deal.

The Autodromo Internacional do Algarve (most commonly referred to as Portimão) is located in Portugal's southernmost region and hosted F1 in 2020 and 2021 during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The 4.6km circuit is an absolute corker as it delivers a technical challenge across dramatic elevation changes amid surrounding historic charm and spectacular beaches.

Oooooh, sounds lovely. Then it must be time for Silverstone?

You guessed right. Silverstone swaps places with Austria to form a double before another double in Belgium and Hungary.

The championship then breaks for the summer for some well-deserved time-off for racing personnel.

We're back in September at Monza, with the Italian race at the historic Temple of Speed forming a double header with Spain's Madring, which will host its second-ever Formula 1 race weekend.

What about the other returning race?

That'll be Türkiye, which makes a return to Formula 1 in the middle of an entertaining triple header with Azerbaijan and Singapore.

The Turkish Grand Prix was last staged in 2020 and 2021, with Lewis Hamilton securing his seventh Drivers' Championship at the venue at Istanbul Park.

The race signed a five-year deal through the 2031 season and is home to the very cool multi-apex Turn 8 that tests a driver's precision and commitment through its long, sweeping left-hander.

Great stuff. Then how does the end of the year look?

It's reassuringly familiar with Austin heading a triple header with Mexico City and Brazil's Sao Paulo before F1 makes its third and final stop in the United States with the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

A Middle Eastern double header in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in December then closes us out.

Domenicali reflects on 'fascinating' season so far

Tasty. The 2027 season can't come soon enough!

We're with you! As I teased earlier, you'll get more qualifying and racing than ever before as the championship is increasing the number of Sprint events from six to 10.

Bahrain, Australia, Japan, Monaco and Abu Dhabi will host the format for the first time. And Canada, Great Britain, Italy, Brazil and Qatar will get another shot to host a Sprint.

You can read more about the Sprint format and plan for next year here.

This is music to our ears. Just one last question - what's the plan for testing?

I’m glad you asked. With new regulations being introduced this year, teams had a five-day Shakedown in Barcelona followed by two three-day tests in Bahrain to prepare for the season.

With continuity in the rules heading into 2027, pre-season testing is reduced to one test, lasting four days in Bahrain at the Bahrain International Circuit at the end of February.

title: Formula 1 reveals calendar for 2027 season
excerpt:
Formula 1 and the FIA have announced, following approval by the World Motor Sport Council, the 2027 FIA Formula One World Championship calendar, featuring 24 Grands Prix across 22 countries and 10 Sprint events.

Pre-season testing will take place in Bahrain from 24–27 February before the Championship returns there for the first race, followed by Saudi Arabia. The calendar then moves to Australia, Japan, and China, followed by the Miami and Canadian Grands Prix.

The European leg includes Formula 1’s return to Portugal in June, after Monaco, with Türkiye rejoining the calendar in October between Azerbaijan and Singapore. The closing phase of the season features races in Austin, Mexico City, Sao Paulo and Las Vegas, before the final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Bringing together historic venues and major global destinations across five continents, the 2027 calendar reflects Formula 1’s continued growth as a global sport and entertainment platform while supporting its long-term sustainability goals through a more efficient geographical flow of events across the season.

Due to the continued success and strong demand for the format, the number of Sprint events has increased from six to 10 for 2027, delivering even more competitive action across the season for fans, promoters, broadcasters, and partners. Since the Sprint was introduced in 2021, the data shows that total viewership of Sprint weekends is 12% higher than non-Sprint weekends. Sprint Qualifying is up to three times more popular with fans than Free Practice, 82% of attendees at Sprint weekends say it adds value to their ticket, and 75% of F1 fans believe Sprint events add greater value to a season’s calendar.

Bahrain, Australia, Japan, Monaco, and Abu Dhabi will host Sprint events for the first time, with fans set to enjoy two thrilling qualifying sessions in Monaco as the drivers show their world class skill and precision on the narrow streets of Monte Carlo. Sprint events will also return to Montreal, Silverstone, Monza, Sao Paulo and Lusail creating even more action-packed race weekends for audiences around the world.

The full 2027 F1 calendar can be viewed below:

Stefano Domenicali, President and CEO of Formula 1, said: “The 2027 calendar brings together some of the most iconic circuits and vibrant cities in the world, creating an incredible stage for another unforgettable season of Formula 1. We are thrilled to welcome Portugal and Türkiye to the championship and to expand Sprint racing to ten events, giving our fans even more intensity, drama, and the wheel-to-wheel action that make our sport so special.

"Formula 1 continues to go from strength-to-strength, attracting new audiences around the globe. Week after week, the world's greatest drivers will battle on some of the most challenging tracks in motorsport, supported by F1’s outstanding teams, world-class manufacturers, and global partners.

"Together, they create a spectacle unlike anything else in sport. As we continue this remarkable journey of growth, I want to thank our fans around the world as their passion drives everything we do.

"I want to thank The President of the FIA, Mohammed Ben Sulayem, and the FIA, our teams and drivers, promoters, partners, sponsors, and host cities for their continued commitment and support and we recognise the extraordinary dedication of the volunteers, marshals, and officials whose hard work makes every Grand Prix possible.

"We are incredibly excited to see this calendar come to life and to deliver another season packed with unforgettable moments, fierce competition, and world-class entertainment for our fans across the globe.”

Everything you need to know about the 2027 Formula 1 calendar

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, added: “The 2027 FIA Formula One World Championship calendar is a strong reflection of the global appeal and continued growth of our sport.

"With 24 Grands Prix across five continents, the return of Portugal and Türkiye, and the opportunity for an expanded Sprint programme, the calendar combines tradition, innovation, and fan engagement while maintaining the highest sporting standards.

“I would like to thank Formula One Management, the promoters, the national sporting authorities, the FIA officials and volunteers and all our stakeholders for their collaboration and commitment.

"Together, we continue to strengthen the FIA Formula One World Championship and deliver an exceptional season for competitors and fans around the world.”

title: Victoria Farfus sets the pace in 2026 F1 ACADEMY Rookie Test
excerpt:
Victoria Farfus topped the timesheets as F1 ACADEMY concluded its 2026 Rookie Test at the Circuito de Navarra.

Designed to give up-and-coming young female drivers the chance to demonstrate their potential for a future full-time seat or Wild Card opportunity on a level playing field, the second edition of the Rookie Test featured an expanded format.

Last month’s Rookie Training Camp at Loughborough University saw the field undertake a range of physical and cognitive assessments alongside interactive workshops to accelerate their development on and off the track.

Following the camp, the drivers gained insights into the demands of competing in the series, immersing themselves within the six F1 ACADEMY teams during the 2026 field’s two days of in-season testing and participated in assessment activities.

The Rookie Test concluded with one day of on-track action. The 18 drivers representing 14 countries got behind the wheel of the F1 ACADEMY machinery, completing 1,447 laps across the board. Farfus secured the fastest overall time, the 15-year-old Brazilian posting a 1:46.988 to finish three tenths clear of Sofia Zanfari and Rosanne Den Drijver in the morning segment.

The afternoon running saw Alexia Danielsson top the timesheets, recording a 1:47.259 in the McLaren OXAGON-liveried car, beating Ella Lähdemaa and Farfus by two tenths. The Rookie Test also featured familiar names such as former 2026 Wild Cards Autumn Fisher and Zoe Florescu, alongside Mercedes junior Luna Fluxa Cross.

The success of the Rookie Test has already been seen, with seven drivers graduating to full-time seats following the inaugural event including Zandvoort Reverse Grid Race winner Payton Westcott and podium finishers Megan Bruce and Natalia Granada.

Katie Denver, Performance & Talent Development Manager, F1 ACADEMY said: “The Rookie Test has been a fantastic opportunity for the rookies to showcase their potential and benchmark themselves against other aspiring drivers and the current F1 ACADEMY grid.

“It has also provided valuable insight into the strengths, development areas and future potential of the next generation of female racing talent. The preparation and commitment shown by all participating drivers throughout the test has been impressive, and we look forward to following their continued progression.”

title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Madrid?
excerpt:
Victory went to Kimi Antonelli at the Spanish Grand Prix after the timing of the Virtual Safety Car scuppered Lando Norris’ efforts. But who impressed our Power Rankings judges over the course of the weekend at the all-new Madring? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below...

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

Norris appeared to do everything right last weekend, bouncing back from technical troubles during Friday practice to take a superb pole position and then surging into a comfortable lead in the early stages of the race. However, a Virtual Safety Car came out at just the wrong time (after he had passed the pit entry) and left him having to settle for P3. Our judges were nonetheless clear on who deserved to top the rankings.

Antonelli was the big beneficiary from Norris’ misfortune – pitting under the VSC himself and taking the lead when Norris stopped. The young Italian continued to impress, however, by comfortably leading the Mercedes charge and ultimately extending his championship lead over team mate George Russell to 81 points.

Max Verstappen gave little away about his and Red Bull’s hopes after a low-key Friday practice in Madrid, but both driver and team stepped forward in Qualifying to come away with a very solid third on the grid. That became second in the race due to Norris’ VSC drama, and a fifth podium finish in the last seven events. “The car is the car, and I think for us to be second is a very good result,” he summed up afterwards.

Franco Colapinto is enjoying a much stronger run at Alpine in 2026, with the Argentinian growing in confidence as he builds experience in the top echelon. The last two events have been particularly encouraging – back-to-back Q3 spots and points being achieved at Monza and in Madrid. After turning ninth on the grid into seventh at the chequered flag on Sunday, he described “probably my best race weekend” in the sport.

Arvid Lindblad looked rapid during Friday practice at Madring, before pushing too hard on a soft-tyre run in FP2 and slamming into the barriers. He rebuilt his confidence, though, to make it through to Q3 and bag more points – his ninth score in the last 10 weekends. Our judges continue to be impressed by the sport’s latest rookie driver.

Battling with Lindblad in the closing stages of Sunday’s race was Nico Hulkenberg, who just missed out on a spot in the final shootout in Qualifying, before edging himself into points contention during a long, hot race in the Spanish capital and coming away with 10th – the German’s third top-10 finish in four events.

While Antonelli and Verstappen pitted under the VSC, and Norris stopped just after it ended, Charles Leclerc extended his opening stint and waited it out for a potential Safety Car. That never came, leaving the Monegasque fourth at the finish, but feeling that there was not much more on the table for himself and Ferrari.

Leclerc was the sole Ferrari driver to make the flag at the Madring after Lewis Hamilton’s early retirement due to brake problems. Hamilton had looked quick in final practice, only to find the wall at the final corner, then led the first Q3 runs before winding up fourth. “I think we had the car to fight for a win today, and unfortunately it just didn’t work out,” he said in the media pen.

After a difficult mid-season run, Esteban Ocon enjoyed a stronger weekend at the Spanish Grand Prix. He was quick in Friday practice, placed 13th in Qualifying and ended the race just outside the points in 11th – while team mate Ollie Bearman got stuck at the back of the field following his heavy crash in FP3 and pit lane start.

Liam Lawson was given a third weekend in the Red Bull in Madrid as Isack Hadjar continues his recovery from a wrist injury. He lacked some confidence during Friday practice but qualified a respectable eighth (not a world away from Verstappen’s lap time) and went on to finish the race in sixth, for his best result at the senior team.

Missing out

Just missing out on a spot in this week’s Power Rankings list is Russell, who started the weekend by topping FP1 but lost confidence as the track conditions improved – meaning he had to settle for sixth in Qualifying and fifth in the Grand Prix.

title: Charles Leclerc provides Ferrari engine update after huge F1 crash
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc is hopeful that Ferrari will be able to save the upgraded engine involved in his huge accident at the Italian Grand Prix.

On Lap 2 at Monza, Leclerc crashed heavily at Parabolica, destroying the Ferrari and triggering a red flag.

The Monegasque was running Ferrari's new ADUO-upgraded engine for the first time at the team's home track, but it was then not in the car for the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid one week later as engineers continue to evaluate the unit to see if it can be used once again.

If it is damaged beyond repair, Leclerc will be forced to take a new example of the ADUO-boosted design, and will thus incur a grid penalty for exceeding his allocation of power unit components.

But he is hopeful this will not prove to be the case.

"For now, of what I know, they're still checking it; we'll see," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365, when asked for an update on the unit.

"I mean, I don't know yet. If we manage to save it, then that's great.

"If not, then probably that's a penalty at some point."

The article continues below.

Leclerc knows where Ferrari must improve its engine

Turning to the Ferrari engine overall, Leclerc felt that the Scuderia needed to make improvements to its one-lap performance in qualifying to help set-up better race-day results.

"For sure, I think our car is a strong race car, but we just need to try and understand how to unlock more performance in qualifying," he said.

"We know that deployment is even more of a struggle, I feel, on a Saturday than on a Sunday, and for that, we don't have any quick fixes.

"But whatever we can do to try and gain a bit of performance on the Saturday would be very helpful for our race result."

title: Lando Norris and McLaren should scare Kimi Antonelli and Mercedes
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli is almost certainly just weeks away from being crowned F1 drivers' champion.

He could, by this stage at least, be aptly described as champion-elect; such is his stranglehold on the standings.

In many ways, it feels like F1 and Antonelli are in this sort of in-between phase, where the title has been decided beyond any reasonable doubt, but now awaits the mere formality of the 20-year-old being coronated.

But success in sport is rare and fleeting, and you don't get to enjoy the moment for long. The greats — at anything, really — quickly turn their attention to what's next. You've scaled that summit, you've conquered that crucible, so what are you going to do now? Or, in the case of a champion, do it again.

This is in no way designed to diminish what will be a campaign for the history books and an achievement he will rightly be handed his flowers for.

But attention will soon turn to the hard work of the close season, and then pre-season, and then, before you know it, it's starting all over again.

There's a championship to win soon becomes there's a championship to retain.

And, as Lando Norris will attest, defending a title is by various measures a more complicated, fraught, and taxing affair.

In theory, it will be somewhat simpler for Antonelli than the McLaren driver has experienced this year, as the F1 regulations remain broadly stable heading into 2027, with no transition from one distinct generation to the next this time around.

At the Madring, for all its flaws, Norris was — for the third time in four rounds — pretty much flawless.

Norris unleashed

However, it's not always so easy when you suddenly find the target now on your back and the opposition closing in.

Even if, somehow, by some freak occurrence or perhaps divine intervention, Antonelli does not manage to get the title over the line, Norris will not be going back-to-back.

His reign is over; his defence is done. 106 points behind the young Italian with only eight or nine rounds to play with, the maths is simply no longer mathsing.

And in many ways, that's fine. Like Antonelli, the 13-time grand prix winner has been superb this season. Results haven't always shown it. Reliability issues and the late-blooming MCL40 have seen to that, but the post-title Norris is clearly operating at a higher level than before, elevated to a higher plane; one reserved, it would seem, for champions.

At the Madring, for all its flaws, Norris was — for the third time in four rounds — pretty much flawless.

And when he's been the fastest guy out there of late, he's crushed the opposition with utter dominance.

In Spain, he was tenths of a second per lap quicker than anyone else. The same at the Hungarian Grand Prix, too.

When he's driving with verve, in a groove with his McLaren, the only thing that can stop him is the virtual safety car.

Winning the title last year unleashed him; freed him from the shackles of self-doubt that seemed at times to be uniquely him — and he knows it.

In recent weeks, Norris has spoken about being able to beat anyone when he has the car to do it, and yeah, at the moment, fair enough.

It's refreshing to see him embrace it, given how much has been made of his honest and self-reflective nature, and he's doing a fine job at emulating what Max Verstappen managed last year, proving that he's every bit the champion the machinery at his disposal might not have shown him to be.

And if he can carry that confidence into 2027, we could be in for one hell of a fight, because McLaren is once again proving to have an innate understanding of how to develop its car.

McLaren's solid platform

The Woking-based squad started the campaign on the back foot, hazed by the lingering hangover necessitated by pouring extra resources into helping Norris claim the very championship he now wears with such casual ease.

And as a power unit customer at the start of a new rules era, it was playing catch-up there too.

Save for the brief hope brought about by his consecutive victories at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort, Norris' title defence really was over before it began — and likewise McLaren’s constructors' crown.

Over the past few years, the team's upgrade philosophy and methodology have consistently delivered sustained gains.

Not only in the sense that the car improves in real terms, and those large developments have been transformative on multiple occasions, but rather the deliberate approach adopted has often meant McLaren is the only top team capable of positive mobility in F1's pecking order of competitiveness. It's how the once-great team returned to the sharp end in the first place.

Those iterations in 2023 and 2024 are well-trodden ground by now, but what differs from this time around, and the updates it brought to Budapest as an example, is that McLaren feels it had the fundamentals of this year's car correct from day one.

"There's a fundamental difference to 2023 — this car that we have at the moment is a solid platform," Stella told me at the Chinese Grand Prix.

"If anything, it's likely underdeveloped; there's nothing in the car that is not sound conceptually. It just needs to be developed further, but following the conceptual lines that we have outlined in the launch phase of this car.

"In 2023, we needed to rectify some designs, pursue some different aerodynamic concepts, because the concept... would not have taken us very far."

So this time, there was no need to change direction, pivot, or claw back lost performance; it started with the right platform, but held off bringing a sophisticated, Spec-A type car — like Mercedes — in favour of a differently considered strategy once the season got going in anger.

And now it's starting to pay dividends, leaving the team in a strong position heading into '27.

Driver

Lando Norris

British

1

On-song and in harmony

In recent rounds, Norris and the MCL40 have been almost perfectly on-song, working in harmony to extract maximum performance.

If you're wondering why I've singled Norris out to take the fight to Antonelli, it's because that unison cannot currently be said of Oscar Piastri in the other McLaren, and he's struggled to match his team-mate's pace all season.

No doubt, the Australian will get there and be able to once again push Norris, but the driving style required of the new cars has meshed better with the latter, and his ability to adapt to the delicate, changing needs of the car, at a stage of the regulations cycle where downforce and mechanical grip are relatively low, which — in addition to being able to Piastri still "thinking and driving", according to Stella — is giving Norris, who is driving more naturally, the edge.

Further aiding McLaren's uptick in results is the strides it has made in tackling the main weakness of the car, low-speed performance.

The team should be heartened by the improvements in that area it made across the weekend at the Madring, through set-up tweaks and alterations.

And if it can address that deficiency in future upgrades, too, the already-solid platform it has will be more consistent and formidable across corner and circuit profiles.

If there is any team on the F1 grid to place faith in its ability to not only turn a situation around, but relentlessly and dependably deliver performance to its car, it's McLaren.

That, paired with a Norris who feels he can win week in, week out, so long as he has the car to do so, will be a powerful combination — and one Antonelli and Mercedes ought to be wary of.

title: Formula E handed F1 headache after 2027 calendar reveal
excerpt:
Formula E has been handed a major clash headache for next year, following the reveal of Formula 1's 2027 calendar.

F1 announced its 24-round calendar for next year on Wednesday morning, with the championship set to travel to 22 countries across the globe over a nine-month period from March to December.

Following its unveiling, clashes with other championships can be identified, in this case with Formula E. The all-electric series' new campaign to kickstart the exciting Gen4 regulatory cycle is currently scheduled to get underway on December 18th, 2026, a fortnight after the current F1 season ends.

Unlike most categories, Formula E's season begins in winter and ends at the end of July during the peak of summer. It will represent the category's 13th season of existence and is its longest yet, spanning 21 races in 11 countries, with eight venues holding double-headers. The calendar was revealed in June.

In total, the Formula E season will take place across 13 weekends, six of which do clash with an F1 Grand Prix. The first clash is Formula E's sixth round in São Paulo and the F1 season-opener in Bahrain in the middle of March, although it is purely a date clash due to the six-hour time difference.

São Paulo in the last two years has clashed with the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, so a clash with a race in the Middle East is nothing new.

What follows is the most significant of the six clashes, as Formula E's Sanya E-Prix falls on the same weekend as the Chinese Grand Prix. It means both series will be in China at the same time.

A direct time zone clash in the same country is far from ideal for Formula E, while it also presents a financial challenge for personnel, teams and media, given that Shanghai was one of many airports used to connect to Sanya.

For the second time in three years, Formula E's Monaco double-header clashes with Miami F1, another clash where the time zone difference makes it more than doable.

The same cannot be said for Formula E's first trip to Zandvoort, which falls on the same weekend as F1's return to Portimao. Only the Friday and Saturday of both events clash, with Formula E taking place a day earlier than usual to allow extra time to head to Madrid the following weekend.

Formula E's final two events of the season in Shanghai and Tokyo also clash with F1, specifically the races in Austria and Spa-Francorchamps. Again, both are in very different time zones, although with Tokyo hosting two night races to end the campaign, it will likely begin just three hours before Belgian GP qualifying and two hours before the race in Spa.

Article continues below...

Formula E issue statement after six F1 clashes discovery

In total, it means that while six Formula E events clash with F1, 10 of the 21 races actually fall on the same day as the elder championship.

Most of the clashes, while frustrating, are manageable due to time zone differences, while the same cannot be said for Zandvoort and, most notably, Shanghai.

RacingNews365 reached out to Formula E for comment on the clashes, with the championship confident that China will ensure both its race in Sanya and F1's in Shanghai will be a success on the same weekend.

In a statement issued to RacingNews365, Formula E co-founder and chief championship officer Alberto Longo said: "Developing a global motorsport calendar always brings unique logistical challenges, particularly given that the majority of both Formula E and Formula 1 races are compressed into the same six-month window.

"While calendar clashes can occur, our experience shows that as long as events take place in different time zones or adhere to different scheduling, they remain perfectly workable for fans and broadcast partners alike.

"Regarding China specifically, Formula E’s calendar was announced in June following approval by our local partner—the Chinese Auto and Moto Sport Federation (CAMF)—as well as the FIA and the World Motor Sport Council.

"We maintain a highly collaborative relationship with local authorities and partners are fully committed to supporting them to ensure our event is a resounding success. Two major world championship motorsport events taking place in the same country at the same time provides double the opportunity for fans to enjoy the pinnacle of racing, and we're looking forward to delivering a fantastic race weekend for our fans in China."

title: Ferrari announce 'exceptional' new 'global leader' F1 sponsor
excerpt:
Scuderia Ferrari HP is pleased to announce a new multi-year global partnership with Rakuten, which will become a Team Partner of the Scuderia in the categories of Telecommunications and E-Commerce from 1 January 2027.

Ferrari has announced a brand-new F1 sponsorship deal with communications giant Rakuten.

Starting from January 1st, 2027, the Japanese "global technology leader" will join forces with the Scuderia, combining Ferrari's "global reach and sporting heritage with Rakuten's technology network and extensive ecosystem."

Away from the track, Rakuten, founded in Tokyo in 1997, Rakuten's "wider ecosystem" will be explored, with "Rakuten Symphony, leveraging the global platform of Formula 1 to develop new business connections, showcase technological capabilities and explore opportunities for cross-industry innovation."

It is not Rakuten's first foray into sports sponsorship, with the company previously being the front of shirt sponsor to Barcelona, adorning the shirts of the likes of Lionel Messi, Neymar, and Luis Suarez between the 2017-18 and 2021-22 seasons.

"Welcoming Rakuten to Scuderia Ferrari is an opportunity to bring together two brands with a strong global presence and a shared belief in the power of innovation," said Lorenzo Giorgetti, Ferrari's chief racing revenue officer.

"Rakuten has built an exceptional digital ecosystem and brings technological capabilities that can open up new ways for us to create value beyond the racetrack.

"We look forward to working together from 2027 and exploring the opportunities that this partnership can create for both our organisations and our communities worldwide."

Meanwhile, the chairman and CEO of the Rakuten Group spoke of the "relentless pursuit of excellence" both companies share.

"Motorsport at the highest level is defined by a relentless pursuit of excellence, in technological innovation and creating unique connections with fans – a commitment we share with Scuderia Ferrari," said Mickey Mikitani.

"This partnership provides a dynamic global stage to bring Rakuten’s technology capabilities, digital ecosystem and unique membership experiences directly to millions of passionate Ferrari and Formula 1 fans around the world."

title: Toto Wolff shares 'grey hair' Kimi Antonelli concern as 'black swan' warning issued
excerpt:
Mercedes boss Toto Wolff has explained how Kimi Antonelli is causing "these grey hairs" with his aggressive driving style in F1.

The Italian now finds himself 81 points clear at the summit and is closing in on shattering the record for the youngest F1 world champion, eclipsing Sebastian Vettel's 2010 record by over three years, if he does go onto win the 2026 crown, as is widely expected.

At the recent Spanish Grand Prix, in the closing stages, Antonelli radioed into his engineer Peter Bonnington to report a potential wall-strike and to ask his W17 be checked for damage, with the 20-year-old pushing hard, despite being in a comfortable lead - which he converted into his eighth win of the season.

Antonelli has a habit of exceeding track limits or running wide and reporting potential wall-strikes, as his Mercedes boss Wolff explained how he and Antonelli's father, Marco, had to "drum" into the protege the danger.

"I just discussed it with his father, and that's just Kimi," Wolff told media, including RacingNews365, when asked about Antonelli's late brush with a wall.

"We had to drum it into his head that he shouldn't go over the white lines, even after Monza [FP1 in 2024] when he went over the white lines and shunted the car.

"I said to him: 'Don't you see out of the car? Do you need to see the high ups that you have the track limits things?'

"We had a laugh about it, and [in the Spanish GP], six laps to the end or whatever it was, he says: 'Check the car, I brushed the wall.'

"He's causing these grey hairs, but maybe he's like this, and maybe that's what is making him so quick."

The article continues below.

Championship talk for Antonelli

With Antonelli 81 points clear of sister Mercedes driver George Russell and over 100 of Lewis Hamilton, barring a calamity, he will be the 2026 world champion.

However, Wolff has urged Antonelli and the team to be careful of a "black swan" event which could snatch the title from his grasp.

"Obviously, he is not thinking about it. This kid is able to compartmentalise and be the young kid and then get into the car and be the mature racing driver," said Wolff.

"That's why Kimi says to himself: 'I'm not thinking about the championship, and he is not thinking about the championship.

"There are black swan events; they can come, and you lose something at the end when you didn't think it was possible to lose."

title: Lando Norris handed unusual reason for Madrid victory escape
excerpt:
Lando Norris missed out on a third victory in four races last time out at the Spanish Grand Prix.

David Coulthard has pointed to an unusual problem that cost Lando Norris victory at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The reigning champion held the lead of the race early on and was in a commanding position as he stretched out his lead over the competition.

However, his event came undone by the timing of a virtual safety car (VSC). Having passed the pit entry after it was deployed, Norris' rivals got a cheap pit stop and jumped ahead of him when the McLaren driver pitted the next time around, right as the VSC ended.

Norris was left to make do with the race in third place, and Coulthard suggested it would have played out much differently for him if he had not been so quick in the first stint.

“Life isn't perfect,” Coulthard told the Up To Speed podcast.

“And what we all agree on is that Lando was unbelievable in the race.

“Here's the problem: he was too quick. Had he been slower, he would have managed to get in under the virtual safety car.

“But because he pulled out that four or five-second lead, he suddenly was the one who was the victim of it. Unlucky for Lando.”

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lando Norris

British

1

Coulthard defends McLaren strategy

Some questioned McLaren's strategy to bring Norris in when he did, as the VSC was coming to an end, knowing he would lose track position.

But Coulthard stated Norris' tyres were nearing the end of their life, making that lap the optimial time to make the pit stop.

“Then they pitted pretty much at the end of the virtual [safety car] to get those medium tyres off because they felt they were not going to go the distance,” he said.

“So they had to pit anyway, and they were going to have to take a full hit.

“So using the gap they would they could get into was the best option for them at that time.

“Plus, they had a bit of a slow stop, the front right wasn't working for them.”

title: Red Bull make Isack Hadjar declaration as injury recovery continues
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has missed the last three grands prix with Red Bull due to a wrist injury.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has insisted the squad will only opt to bring Isack Hadjar back to his race seat when it is comfortable that his return is risk-free.

Hadjar suffered a wrist injury during the summer break, ruling himself out of the following three rounds.

In his absence, Liam Lawson has stepped in while Yuki Tsunoda replaced the New Zealander at Racing Bulls.

With the upcoming weekend being an off-weekend for F1, it offers Hadjar some extra time to recover in the hope of getting back behind the wheel in Baku.

But while the delay goes on, Mekies asserted nothing is amiss with the timeline for his return.

“There is nothing wrong with Isack's recovery,” Mekies told media including RacingNews365.

“I think we have learned that it's fundamentally a normal time for the sort of injuries he has.

“So we will continue with the same approach than what we had.

“We will evaluate the situation in a week's time. We have a bit more than a full week to evaluate the situation, to see how he feels.”

[Article continues below]

Driver

Isack Hadjar

French

6

Hadjar set for simulator sessions ahead of final call

Hadjar had been enjoying a positive first season inside the Red Bull team this year, and was a frequent finisher inside the top six.

While he is no doubt itching for the chance to race once again, Mekies proclaimed that the team will not risk aggravating the injury by rushing him back.

“Then [we plan] to put him on the simulator, to expose him to real-life constraints,” he said.

“If he feels close to 100%, we go for it. If he feels the recovery is not completed, we will stick to our approach to put his recovery first.

“What we don't want to do is, by having an early return, compromise his long-term capacity to come back to 100 per cent.”

title: Max Verstappen blitzes field in chaotic race against 100 opponents
excerpt:
Max Verstappen eased his way to the front of the field in a chaotic karting event hosted by Red Bull at Silverstone on Wednesday.

Verstappen faced off against 100 opponents consisting of various online personalities and Red Bull athletes.

The Dutchman lined up at the back of the field, with the premise being that once he moved in front of a competitor, they dropped out of the race.

But with 100 karts fighting for the same piece of track on the opening lap, chaos ensued with multiple collisions occurring.

Verstappen also cut the track and found himself in P36, eliminating almost two-thirds of the pack on lap one.

From there, the four-time champion picked his way through the field, with his progress getting slower as he climbed the pack and came across the more competitive rivals.

35 minutes after the race start, Verstappen overtook his final competitor to complete the challenge.

“That was simply lovely, wasn't it?” Verstappen said immediately after it was over.

“I really thought my first lap would be a disaster, but I got helped a little bit with people getting super excited and crashing.

“That helped, a little bit - but it was a lot of fun.”

excerpt:
Max Verstappen faces arguably his most unusual challenge yet this evening as he lines up last on a 101-kart grid at Silverstone, tasked with overtaking all 100 drivers ahead of him within 30 laps.

The Red Bull star will start from P101 on a purpose-built kart circuit, with identical machinery for every competitor.

The 100 challengers, a mix of athletes, content creators and fans, will do everything they can to keep Verstappen behind.

Each driver he passes is eliminated, but there is a twist: the challengers can each use a track shortcut once in the first 15 laps, while Verstappen can only deploy his after half distance.

The win condition is simple but brutal: pass all 100 or fail. The race gets underway at 6pm.

title: Haas facing final evaluation as 2027 line-up decision nears
excerpt:
The Haas F1 team will carry out a test later this week as it closes in on a decision over its driver line-up for the 2027 season.

While Oliver Bearman is widely expected to continue with Haas for a third-straight season, the identity of his team-mate has not yet been confirmed.

Currently in the second seat is Esteban Ocon, who joined the American squad last year following a stint at Alpine.

As the team mulls over its options, fresh contenders have emerged - including Formula 2 championship contender Rafael Camara.

It has been rumoured that Camara is in the strongest position of all contenders to obtain a seat and step up to F1 as a rookie driver next year.

However, RacingNews365 understands that no such decision will be made until after Haas conducts a TPC (testing of previous cars) run at Jerez later this week.

On Thursday, Jack Doohan will get behind the wheel as the team evaluates his potential for a promotion next year.

Doohan has seven grand prix starts in his career with Alpine, but was dropped from a race seat shortly after the start of 2025 campaign in favour of Franco Colapinto.

At the start of 2026, Doohan joined Haas as a reserve driver in a bid to get himself back onto the grid.

While it seems Camara is in the better position as things stand, it is a challenging decision for the team to make, as his promotion would see Haas field two Ferrari juniors.

It is understood would bring some financial backing to Haas, but the team would effectively be without its own in-house competitor, with Ferrari having ultimate control over their futures.

Finally, one outside option for Haas is its development driver, Ryo Hirakawa.

The Japanese driver has taken part in multiple FP1 outings with Haas over the last two years as part of the team's relationship with Toyota Gazoo Racing.

However, paddock voices suggest that Hirakawa's chances are minimal at best.

title: Cadillac deliver Sergio Perez response after 'disappointment' verdict
excerpt:
Sergio Perez recently voiced his disappointment with the form on display from the Cadillac team.

Cadillac team principal Marcin Budkowski has issued a response to Sergio Perez after the Mexican voiced “disappointment” over the squad's form.

The American outfit joined the grid as an 11th team this year and immediately placed at the back of the field as it got up to speed in the sport.

Following a difficult period in recent events, Perez has stated there has been “a lot of disappointment” within the team due to the lack of progress.

But Budkowski, who took over at the helm of the team from Graeme Lowdon midway through the campaign, stated he informed Perez that he needed to keep his expectations in check.

When asked by media including RacingNews365 if the team has reached a development plateau, Budkowski said: “No.

“I think you have to put that in perspective with the drivers’ expectations and the reality of the seasonality of F1.

“Before I even started, after my appointment was announced, I had a quick chat with both drivers.

“And Sergio asked me, 'What are you going to do for Zandvoort?', which is a week after I started. And I said, 'Well, Checo, I think I need to control the expectations a little bit.'”

Cadillac has switched focus to 2027 F1 car

While Cadillac has been located at the back of the field thus far, it has also battled several reliability issues, particularly regarding its brakes.

Addressing its struggling form, Budkowski detailed that Cadillac's performance has taken a knock due to applying resources to fix such concerns, as well focus now being switched to the 2027 challenger.

“The reality is we’re in a phase of the season where we’re all working on next year’s car,” he said.

“We’ve switched the resources mostly to next year. We have a development pipeline that’s slowly drying out.

“A lot of our resources have also been, unfortunately, busy fixing our reliability issues rather than working on performance items. So naturally, the development is plateauing in this phase of the season.

“But I think on our side, we have a lot of potential through fixing the reliability, fixing the operational side, fixing the quality of the car.

“There’s performance there that we can still extract this year. But our focus needs to be on next year’s car, and I think everybody will tell you this up and down the pit lane.”

title: Aston Martin fear 'dramatic' unthinkable over Fernando Alonso
excerpt:
Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack believes it would be “unthinkable” and "dramatic" if Fernando Alonso opted to quit the team and F1 at the end of this season.

Alonso is weighing up his future at a time when Aston Martin is suffering on track after a major change to this year's regulations, and also in taking on a new power unit partner after joining forces with Honda and ending its prior partnership with Mercedes.

The two-time F1 champion has made clear he will not be rushed into making a decision, primarily as he waits to see if the team can continue to make gains over the remainder of the season after taking a step in the right direction recently. Honda, however, is still struggling.

Krack can appreciate why Alonso is biding his time.

"At the end of the day, we have always been clear that the team wants to continue [with him], but we need to respect what Fernando's thoughts are and the time he wants to take," he said, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"As I've said before, we're confident we can reach a good solution for everybody. Now it's about waiting. He needs to make up his mind, and then we move on."

Alonso has additionally made clear his dislike of the regulations, describing F1 as "a battery world championship".

Last weekend in Madrid, the new home of the Spanish Grand Prix, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has stated that he plans to talk with Alonso to convince him to stay, and that he should not end his remarkable F1 career with a season like this.

"He has made clear that it is not one single thing that he wants to see change," said Krack. "And yeah, I read about these discussions [with Ben Sulayem] as well. The sport needs someone like that.

"We will all be keen to see Fernando continue. What can be done to accommodate, I think, it will be done, and then I hope we can come to a good solution and continue."

[Article continues below]

Aston Martin refusing to discuss 'plan B'

At this stage, Krack is refusing to divulge whether the team has contingency plans should Alonso opt to quit, believing it has time on its side.

"I will not give you any names [of a potential replacement], and I will also not speak about any plan B," he said.

"We very much hope that Fernando will continue. He's very important for our team, very important for Formula 1, and motorsport in general."

As to the alternative, however, that is a possibility Krack does not want to consider.

"It would be a pity to not have him anymore," he said.

"And because that would be so dramatic, I do not even want to talk about it or think about it."
